Consensus with births and deaths over contact types: the resting scenes of a mug and a spoon

Abstract. We propose a way to find the families of resting scenes of a mug and a spoon on a table, starting from uniformly random placements only. Particles of polarised consensus-based optimisation move through the touching scenes of an interaction collar, in which one body is lowered onto the table and the other onto whatever lies below it. A particle is scored by how far a one-second simulated release carries its scene and by how far the scene ends from contact. Two particles count as near only if their scenes start near each other and end near each other, with distances measured through the mug's opening rather than through its wall. To keep rare kinds of contact from being absorbed by common ones, the population is redistributed over contact types by births and deaths. The resting scenes the run returns are grouped into components by sampled paths of resting scenes.

1. The scenes and the search space

We want to arrange a mug and a spoon on a table so that, when released, they stay where they are. Such arrangements come in families. The spoon can lie on the table against the mug, lean on it with its foot on the table, rest across its rim, stand in its cup or have only its handle in the cup, and the mug itself can stand upright, lie on its side or stand upside down. We are interested in the arrangements in which the two bodies touch, and the aim is to hold scenes from as many of these families as possible in one population of particles.

1.1 Scenes, poses and the table gauge

To describe one arrangement, first fix a coordinate system to each body. A point \(p\in\mathbb R^3\) then identifies the same material point of that body wherever it is placed. Its position in the world is determined by a rotation matrix \(R_b\) and a translation vector \(t_b\), where \(b\) denotes the mug or the spoon. Rotation matrices satisfy

$$SO(3)=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^\top R=I_3,\ \det R=1\},$$

where \(I_3\) is the three-dimensional identity matrix. A scene \(s\) consists of both poses, and the world position of the material point \(p\) of body \(b\) in that scene is

$$s=\bigl((R_{\text{mug}},t_{\text{mug}}),(R_{\text{spoon}},t_{\text{spoon}})\bigr),\qquad y_b(p;s)=R_bp+t_b.$$

The table is the plane \(z=0\), and \(e_z=(0,0,1)\) is the upward direction. Moving the entire scene horizontally, or turning it as a whole about the vertical, leaves the physical problem unchanged. These motions form a group, the table gauge. Write \(R_z(\psi)\) for the rotation by the angle \(\psi\) about the vertical axis \(e_z\). For a horizontal shift \(a=(a_1,a_2)\) and a turn \(\psi\), the gauge element \(\gamma_{a,\psi}\) moves both bodies with the same horizontal rigid motion:

$$\Gamma=\bigl\{\gamma_{a,\psi}:\ a\in\mathbb R^2,\ \psi\in(-\pi,\pi]\bigr\},\qquad \gamma_{a,\psi}\cdot s=\Bigl(\bigl(R_z(\psi)R_b,\ R_z(\psi)\,t_b+(a_1,a_2,0)\bigr)\Bigr)_{b\in\{\text{mug},\,\text{spoon}\}}.$$

Every material point moves by that motion, \(y_b(p;\gamma_{a,\psi}\cdot s)=R_z(\psi)\,y_b(p;s)+(a_1,a_2,0)\), so distances between points and heights above the table are unchanged. Two scenes related by an element of \(\Gamma\) are physically the same. We call the set \(\{\gamma\cdot s:\gamma\in\Gamma\}\) the gauge class of \(s\), and for a set of scenes \(\mathcal Y\) that the gauge maps onto itself we write \(\mathcal Y/\Gamma\) for the set of its gauge classes. The group has three parameters.

1.2 The bodies as point clouds

To decide whether two placed bodies overlap, and how far a body can be lowered before it meets something, we need the shape of each body in a form in which these questions can be answered quickly and exactly. We describe each body by two finite point sets, fixed once in its own coordinates.

The first samples its surface. For body \(b\), let \(q_{b,1},\ldots,q_{b,n_b}\) be points spread uniformly over the exposed surface of its geometric primitives, and let \(\nu_{b,k}\) be the outward unit normal at \(q_{b,k}\). There are \(n_{\text{mug}}=131\,072\) points on the mug and \(n_{\text{spoon}}=32\,768\) on the spoon, so neighbouring points are about a millimetre apart.

The second covers the solid by balls. At every surface sample we place a ball that touches the surface from inside at that point, so its centre lies on the inward normal:

$$c_{b,k}=q_{b,k}-\rho_{b,k}\,\nu_{b,k},\qquad 0\lt\rho_{b,k}\le1.5\ \text{mm}.$$

Its radius \(\rho_{b,k}\) is the largest value up to the cap for which no other surface sample lies inside the ball and the ball stays on the inner side of the tangent planes of nearby samples; most of these balls reach the cap. The interior that they do not reach is filled with further balls centred on a regular grid, each with a radius bounded by its distance to the surface. Writing \(\bar B(c,\rho)\) for the closed ball of centre \(c\) and radius \(\rho\), the occupied region of body \(b\) in its own coordinates is the finite union

$$\mathcal U_b=\bigcup_{k=1}^{m_b}\bar B\bigl(c_{b,k},\rho_{b,k}\bigr),\qquad m_{\text{mug}}=224\,849,\quad m_{\text{spoon}}=34\,765,$$

where the first \(n_b\) balls are the surface balls and the others fill the interior. In a scene \(s\) the body occupies \(\mathcal U_b(s)=\{R_by+t_b:\ y\in\mathcal U_b\}\). A rigid motion carries a ball to a ball of the same radius, so this is again a union of balls, with centres \(y_b(c_{b,k};s)=R_bc_{b,k}+t_b\) and unchanged radii.

1.3 Admissible and touching scenes

With balls, every question about contact reduces to distances between centres. Two balls overlap exactly when their centres are closer than the sum of their radii, and a ball lies above the table exactly when its centre is at least one radius above it. A scene is admissible when no ball of one body overlaps a ball of the other and every ball lies above the table:

$$\mathcal A=\Bigl\{s:\ \bigl\|y_{\text{mug}}(c_{\text{mug},k};s)-y_{\text{spoon}}(c_{\text{spoon},l};s)\bigr\|\ge\rho_{\text{mug},k}+\rho_{\text{spoon},l}\ \text{ for all }k,l,\ \ \ e_z\cdot y_b(c_{b,k};s)\ge\rho_{b,k}\ \text{ for all }b,k\Bigr\}.$$

Among the admissible scenes we want those in which no body floats. A body is supported from below when lowering it alone, by any distance however small, would make it overlap the table or the other body. Writing \(s-\varepsilon e_z^{(b)}\) for the scene in which body \(b\) is moved down by \(\varepsilon\) and the other body is left in place, the touching scenes are

$$\mathcal S=\Bigl\{s\in\mathcal A:\ s-\varepsilon e_z^{(b)}\notin\mathcal A\ \text{ for every }\varepsilon\gt0\text{ and both bodies }b\Bigr\}.$$

A body standing on the table or resting on the other body passes this test; a body hovering above everything fails it. Every resting scene lies in \(\mathcal S\), except scenes in which a body is held up only by friction against vertical walls. Because the gauge preserves distances between ball centres and their heights above the table, it maps \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal S\) onto themselves, and the touching scenes up to the gauge form the set \(\mathcal S/\Gamma\). This is the set we search.

A placement chosen at random almost never lies in \(\mathcal S\): it floats or overlaps, and when it is let go the bodies mostly fall or are pushed apart, which says little about how they could rest. So rather than placing the bodies freely and testing, we describe touching scenes directly. We choose how the bodies are turned and where the spoon stands horizontally relative to the mug, and lower each body onto what lies below it.

1.4 Orientations without the gauge

Start with the mug. If the mug is turned about the vertical, nothing changes physically, so its world rotation contains one angle too many. What does matter is which way is down for the mug. Express the downward direction in the mug's own coordinates:

$$u=R_{\text{mug}}^\top(-e_z),\qquad u\in S^2=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\|v\|=1\}.$$

For example, an upright mug has \(R_{\text{mug}}=I_3\), so \(u=(0,0,-1)\): its own downward axis points down. An upside-down mug has \(u=(0,0,1)\), and a mug on its side has a \(u\) with zero third component. A gauge turn replaces \(R_{\text{mug}}\) by \(R_z(\psi)R_{\text{mug}}\); since \(R_z(\psi)^\top e_z=e_z\), the vector \(u\) is unchanged. The attitude \(u\) is therefore a point of the unit sphere that carries no table gauge.

Next, the spoon. Its families are defined by how it lies relative to the mug, so we describe its orientation in the mug's coordinates:

$$R=R_{\text{mug}}^\top R_{\text{spoon}}\in SO(3).$$

A gauge turn multiplies both world rotations by the same \(R_z(\psi)\), which cancels in \(R\). A change of the mug's attitude with \(R\) held fixed carries the spoon along with the mug, as if the two were glued, which is what we want when the spoon is already in a good place relative to the mug.

The pair \((u,R)\) fixes both orientations up to a turn of the whole scene about the vertical. To build world rotations we pick one representative: the smallest rotation that carries the mug's \(u\) to the world's downward direction. Writing \(v=u\times(-e_z)\) and \(c=u\cdot(-e_z)\), Rodrigues' formula gives

$$R_{\text{mug}}=S(u)=I_3+[v]_\times+\frac{[v]_\times^2}{1+c},\qquad R_{\text{spoon}}=S(u)\,R,$$

where \([v]_\times\) is the skew matrix with \([v]_\times a=v\times a\). (For \(u=e_z\), where \(c=-1\), a half turn about the \(x\) axis is used.) Any other choice differs by a gauge turn of the whole scene.

1.5 Lowering a body onto what lies below

Suppose now that both orientations are fixed and that the horizontal position of each body's centre of mass is given. One body is lowered first, onto the table; the other is lowered second, onto the first body and the table. Consider the body lowered first, say the mug, with its centre of mass at height \(h\). Since \(-u\) is the world's upward direction written in the mug's coordinates, its ball \(k\) has its lowest point at height \(h-\langle c_{\text{mug},k}-c_{\text{mug}},u\rangle-\rho_{\text{mug},k}\), where \(c_{\text{mug}}\) is the mug's centre of mass. The mug touches the table without entering it when the lowest of these heights is zero, that is, at

$$h_{\text{mug}}=\max_{k\le m_{\text{mug}}}\Bigl(\bigl\langle c_{\text{mug},k}-c_{\text{mug}},\,u\bigr\rangle+\rho_{\text{mug},k}\Bigr),$$

the support function of its cloud in the downward direction: the largest extent of the cloud in that direction, since a ball of centre \(c\) and radius \(\rho\) extends to \(\langle c,v\rangle+\rho\) in a direction \(v\), and a union of balls extends as far as its furthest member. With the spoon first, the same formula is applied to the spoon, whose downward direction in its own coordinates is \(R^\top u\).

The body lowered second moves down its vertical line onto the first body and the table. With its orientation and horizontal position fixed, let \(h\) be the height of its centre of mass and \(x_k+h\,e_z\) the centre of its ball \(k\), where \(x_k\) is the centre at \(h=0\). A ball \(l\) of the first body, already placed, has centre \(y_l\). The two balls overlap exactly when \(\|x_k+he_z-y_l\|\lt\rho_k+\rho_l\). Split the difference into a horizontal part of length \(d_{kl}\) and the vertical part \(h-\Delta_{kl}\), with \(\Delta_{kl}=e_z\cdot(y_l-x_k)\); the condition becomes \((h-\Delta_{kl})^2\lt(\rho_k+\rho_l)^2-d_{kl}^2\). So the pair forbids no height when \(d_{kl}\ge\rho_k+\rho_l\), and otherwise exactly the open interval

$$I_{kl}=\bigl(\Delta_{kl}-\chi_{kl},\ \Delta_{kl}+\chi_{kl}\bigr),\qquad \chi_{kl}=\sqrt{(\rho_k+\rho_l)^2-d_{kl}^2}.$$

The table adds the lower bound \(h\ge h_0=\max_k\bigl(\rho_k-e_z\cdot x_k\bigr)\). The admissible heights form the closed set \([h_0,\infty)\setminus\bigcup_{k,l}I_{kl}\), a finite union of intervals, and the body is placed at its smallest element:

$$h_{\text{second}}=\min\Bigl([h_0,\infty)\setminus\bigcup_{k,l}I_{kl}\Bigr).$$

Sorting the intervals and sweeping upward from \(h_0\) finds this height exactly. Because the sweep stops at the bottom of the lowest free interval, a spoon that fits inside the cup, or under an upside-down mug, is placed there rather than stopped at the rim. With both heights found the scene is admissible, and both bodies are supported: the first by the table, the second by whatever ends the forbidden interval below it, or by the table. The result is a touching scene.

1.6 The interaction collar

It remains to choose the horizontal offset \(w\) of the spoon's centre of mass from the mug's. Seen from the mug, the horizontal plane is the plane orthogonal to \(u\). Far-apart offsets are of little interest: there the bodies simply rest on the table side by side. To see where interaction begins, project each body vertically onto the table and take the convex hull of its shadow; write \(K_{\text{mug}}\) and \(K_{\text{spoon}}\) for these hulls, measured from each body's centre of mass. With the spoon's centre of mass at offset \(w\), the two hulls overlap exactly when some point lies in both, that is, when \(k_{\text{mug}}=w+k_{\text{spoon}}\) for some \(k_{\text{mug}}\in K_{\text{mug}}\) and \(k_{\text{spoon}}\in K_{\text{spoon}}\). Rearranged, the hulls overlap exactly when

$$w\in K=K_{\text{mug}}+(-K_{\text{spoon}}),$$

the set of differences between a point of the first hull and a point of the second. This is a convex set containing the origin. A convex set is described by its support function, its largest extent in a given direction, and the support function of a sum is the sum of the support functions. For the ball clouds the support function is the one already used in Section 1.5, and projecting vertically does not change the extent in a horizontal direction. For a unit horizontal direction \(e\), a direction orthogonal to \(u\) in the mug's frame, the support function of \(K\) is therefore

$$H(e)=\max_{k\le m_{\text{mug}}}\Bigl(\bigl\langle c_{\text{mug},k}-c_{\text{mug}},\,e\bigr\rangle+\rho_{\text{mug},k}\Bigr)+\max_{l\le m_{\text{spoon}}}\Bigl(\bigl\langle R\,(c_{\text{spoon},l}-c_{\text{spoon}}),\,-e\bigr\rangle+\rho_{\text{spoon},l}\Bigr).$$

Only balls on the convex hull of a cloud can attain a maximum; these are found once, and \(H\) then costs a few hundred inner products. We describe the offset by a point \(\xi\) of the unit disc in the horizontal plane, stretched radially onto \(K\):

$$\bar D_u=\bigl\{\xi\in\mathbb R^3:\ \xi\cdot u=0,\ \|\xi\|\le1\bigr\},\qquad w(\xi)=H\!\left(\frac{\xi}{\|\xi\|}\right)\xi,\quad w(0)=0.$$

So \(\|\xi\|=1\) means that the spoon stands just beside the mug in that direction, and \(\xi=0\) that the centres of mass are vertically aligned. Three properties follow from convexity alone. First, every offset at which the hulls overlap is reached: in each direction, the boundary of a convex set containing the origin lies no further out than its support function, so the stretched disc covers \(K\). Second, an offset with \(\|\xi\|=1\) lies on a supporting line of \(K\), so the two hulls at most touch and the upper body is lowered onto the table beside the lower one. Third, offsets beyond \(K\) carry no information at all. Once the shadows are further apart than either body can travel when it is let go, the bodies cannot meet: letting the scene go is the same as letting each body go alone, and the outcome does not depend on how far apart they are. The far field is therefore represented once, by the boundary circle.

The size of the collar follows the orientations. For an upright mug and a spoon standing nearly vertical, \(H\) is about 63 mm on the side away from the handle (the mug's outer radius of 49 mm plus 14 mm for the spoon), and more on the handle side. The bowl falls into the cup when the spoon's centre of mass is within about 27 mm of the mug's axis, which is roughly 15 % of the collar. A flat spoon has a wide collar, because it can reach the mug from far away; a steep spoon has a narrow one.

1.7 The search space

Finally, a real coordinate \(p\) chooses which body is lowered first: the mug if \(p\ge0\), the spoon otherwise. Together these form the particle state

$$x=(p,u,\xi,R),\qquad p\in\mathbb R,\quad (u,\xi)\in\mathcal C,\quad R\in SO(3),$$

and the search space is the product

$$\mathcal X=\mathbb R\times\mathcal C\times SO(3),\qquad \mathcal C=\Bigl\{(u,\xi)\in S^2\times\mathbb R^3:\ \xi\cdot u=0,\ \ \|\xi\|\le1\Bigr\}.$$

We call \(\mathcal C\) the interaction collar: over every attitude \(u\) of the mug it carries the disc \(\bar D_u\) of offsets. A point of \(\mathcal X\) is turned into a scene by the steps of Sections 1.4 to 1.6: the orientations \(S(u)\) and \(S(u)R\), the offset \(w(\xi)\), and the two heights of the lowering in the order given by \(p\). We call this construction \(T\):

$$T:\ \mathcal X\longrightarrow\mathcal S/\Gamma,\qquad T(x)=\bigl((S(u),t_{\text{mug}}),\,(S(u)R,t_{\text{spoon}})\bigr).$$

Counting coordinates, \(u\) has two, \(\xi\) two and \(R\) three, so seven numbers describe a touching scene, besides the order. This is the dimension of \(\mathcal S/\Gamma\): two rigid bodies have twelve degrees of freedom, being supported fixes the two heights, and the three parameters of the table gauge remove three. The map does not reach all of \(\mathcal S\). It places the second body at the lowest admissible height on its vertical line, so it misses scenes in which a body rests above an empty pocket into which it would fit; it reaches every other touching scene. The particles move continuously in \(\mathcal X\). The clouds are not a grid of positions, but they decide where every coordinate value leads. Computing \(T\) uses only the clouds: it does not advance a physics simulation or let the bodies settle, so a touching placement may still topple or slide.

2. Fornasier–Sun polarised consensus-based optimisation

With the search space specified, we can say how a population of particles is to move through it. The reference is the polarised consensus model of Massimo Fornasier and Lukang Sun. Consider first its Euclidean form. For particles \(z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^d\) and a nonnegative objective \(f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\), its empirical particle equation is

$$dz_i=-\lambda(z_i-m_i)\,dt+\sigma\bigl(\|z_i-m_i\|+\kappa\bigr)\,dB_i.$$

Here \(t\) is optimisation time, \(B_i\) are independent standard \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motions, \(\lambda>0\) sets the strength of attraction and \(\sigma\ge0\) that of diffusion. The constant \(\kappa\ge0\) is an exploration floor: it keeps a particle moving even when it sits on its consensus point. The point \(m_i\) is a weighted consensus for particle \(i\), in which other particles are favoured both for scoring well under \(f\) and for being near \(z_i\). Because those weights depend on \(i\), different parts of the population can follow different consensus points, and this is what lets one population hold several families at once.

To define the consensus, Fornasier and Sun give source particle \(z_j\) the affinity

$$A_f(z_j,z_i)=f(z_j)\bigl(f(z_i)+\theta\bigr)+\|z_i-z_j\|^2,\qquad\theta>0,$$

where we have absorbed their relative scale into the units of \(f\). The first term favours sources with a smaller objective, with a strength set by the receiving particle's own objective; the second favours nearby sources. A positive inverse temperature \(\alpha_i\) turns affinities into weights and a consensus point:

$$w_{ij}=\exp[-\alpha_iA_f(z_j,z_i)],\qquad m_i=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^Nw_{ij}z_j}{\sum_{j=1}^Nw_{ij}}.$$

The weighted mean is the point that minimises the weighted sum of squared distances to the sources. Holding the weights fixed and setting the derivative to zero,

$$m_i=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{m\in\mathbb R^d}\sum_jw_{ij}\|m-z_j\|^2,\qquad 0=2\sum_jw_{ij}(m_i-z_j),$$

and solving the last equation gives the displayed formula. This characterisation needs only a way to measure squared distances to the sources, not a way to add points together.

Comparing a source's affinity with the particle's own shows what the two terms negotiate. Since \(\|z_i-z_i\|=0\), particle \(j\) receives more weight than \(i\) gives itself exactly when

$$A_f(z_j,z_i)\lt A_f(z_i,z_i)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\|z_i-z_j\|^2\lt\bigl(f(z_i)-f(z_j)\bigr)\bigl(f(z_i)+\theta\bigr).$$

A source must improve the objective enough to justify its distance. Because \(f(z_j)\ge0\), no source further than \(\rho_i=\sqrt{(f(z_i)+\theta)f(z_i)}\) can outweigh the particle itself. We call \(\rho_i\) the particle's reach. A particle at a minimum, \(f(z_i)=0\), has reach zero: nothing can pull it away, which is the property that makes the model polarised.

3. Scene simulation

We now have a scene \(s=T(x)\) to test. Both bodies are given zero initial velocity and released for \(H_\tau=1\) second in MuJoCo, with friction 0.6 and a time step of \(\Delta\tau=2\) ms. The release model adds a light viscous drag, which relaxes free motion of the spoon and the mug's rotation with a time constant of 0.1 s, so that a scene that is nearly at rest settles within the second. Writing \(\tau\) for simulation time, the trajectory is

$$s_\tau=\bigl((R_b(\tau;s),t_b(\tau;s))\bigr)_b,\qquad s_0=s,\quad 0\le\tau\le H_\tau.$$

The first observation is where the release ends. The function \(e\) returns the poses at the end:

$$e(s)=s_{H_\tau}.$$

These are endpoint poses; the bodies may still be moving at time \(H_\tau\). We also want to know how far they moved on the way, since a body could move off and come back. For this the observer follows a fixed set \(K_b\) of material points on each body, and records the largest displacement of any of them from its starting position:

$$X_b(s)=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal T}\max_{p\in K_b}\bigl\|y_b(\tau,p;s)-y_b(0,p;s)\bigr\|,\qquad \mathcal T=\{0,\Delta\tau,2\Delta\tau,\ldots,H_\tau\},$$

with \(y_b(\tau,p;s)=R_b(\tau;s)p+t_b(\tau;s)\). This is the greatest excursion from the starting position, not the length of a point's path, and because the observer uses finite point sets and time steps it approximates the maximum over the whole body and the continuous release.

The soft-contact simulation can also let shapes overlap. The collision detector reports the depth of each contact; let \(\delta_0(s)\) be the greatest depth in the starting placement and \(\delta(s)\) the greatest depth during the release. Both have units of length. Together, the endpoint \(e(s)\), the excursions \(X_b(s)\) and the two depths describe what happened to the scene when it was released.

4. A metric for comparing scenes

To use the release we need a way to say how far the final scene is from the starting one; the consensus of Section 2 also needs a distance between particles, and one comparison serves both. A distance between body centres alone would miss rotations, so we compare corresponding material points instead. And because the table gauge must not count, we compare them as seen from the mug.

For this we use the surface samples of Section 1.2, written relative to each body's centre of mass: \(P_b=\{q_{b,k}-c_b\}_{k=1}^{n_b}\). In this section \(q\) denotes such a relative sample. Consider the spoon first. In a scene \(s\), its point \(q\) sits, in the mug's coordinates, at \(R\,q+c\), where \(c\) is the spoon's centre of mass in the mug's coordinates. Between two scenes \(s\) and \(s'\), the mean squared displacement of the spoon's points as seen from the mug is

$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{q\in P_{\text{spoon}}}\bigl\|(Rq+c)-(R'q+c')\bigr\|^2 .$$

This can be evaluated without moving every sample point. Write \(a=\frac1n\sum_qq\) for the samples' centroid and \(S^2=\frac1n\sum_q(q-a)(q-a)^\top\) for their covariance, with \(S\) its symmetric positive semidefinite square root. Splitting \(q=a+(q-a)\), the cross terms average to zero because the deviations \(q-a\) do, and

$$\begin{aligned} \frac1n\sum_q\bigl\|(R-R')q+(c-c')\bigr\|^2 &=\bigl\|(R-R')a+(c-c')\bigr\|^2+\frac1n\sum_q\bigl\|(R-R')(q-a)\bigr\|^2\\ &=\bigl\|\bar c-\bar c'\bigr\|^2+\bigl\|(R-R')S\bigr\|_F^2, \end{aligned}$$

where \(\bar c=Ra+c\) is the centroid of the spoon's samples in the mug's coordinates and \(\|\cdot\|_F^2\) is the sum of squared matrix entries. The last step uses \(\frac1n\sum_q\|Mv_q\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(M S^2M^\top)=\|MS\|_F^2\) for \(v_q=q-a\). So the spoon's displacement is captured exactly by twelve numbers: the centroid \(\bar c\) and the nine entries of \(RS\).

For the mug, its own coordinates cannot see it move. What changes between two scenes is its attitude and the height of its centre of mass. A tilt of the mug by the small angle between \(u\) and \(u'\) moves its surface points by roughly the tilt angle times their distance from the centre of mass, so we weight the chord \(\|u-u'\|\) by the root-mean-square radius \(r_{\text{mug}}\) of the mug's samples. Collecting everything gives the material embedding

$$\Psi(s)=\bigl(r_{\text{mug}}\,u,\ z_{\text{mug}},\ \bar c,\ R\,S\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{3+1+3+9},$$

with \(z_{\text{mug}}\) the height of the mug's centre of mass. Every entry is unchanged by the table gauge. The distance between scenes is the Euclidean distance between their embeddings,

$$d(s,s')=\|\Psi(s)-\Psi(s')\|,$$

which has units of length. Its spoon part is the exact mean squared displacement of the spoon's surface seen from the mug; its mug part is an isotropic stand-in for the mug's own displacement.

Distances across the mug's wall

The distance \(d\) treats space as empty: it measures the straight line that each material point would travel. Most of the time that is harmless. It goes wrong in one important place. A spoon lying inside the mug on its side and a spoon lying outside the mug against the same wall are only about 2 cm apart in \(d\), yet no motion of the spoon can carry one into the other without leaving through the opening, because the wall is in the way. A particle in the cup would then count a particle outside as a close neighbour, and the consensus would pull it through the wall.

The honest distance is the length of the shortest motion of the spoon that keeps all its material out of the mug. Measuring that is a motion-planning problem, far too expensive for the \(10^8\) pairs of particles compared at each update. We can, however, bound it from below by something cheap. The idea is to look at one material point at a time. Every path that takes a point from inside the cup to outside must pass through the cup's opening: if it never left the hull of the mug, it would stay in the cup, because the wall separates the cup from everything else inside the hull. So the point travels at least the length of the shortest route through the opening. Replace the opening by the whole plane \(z=z_L\) of the rim, which only admits more routes, and the shortest route has a closed form. Let \(x\) be inside the cup, at depth \(a=z_L-z_x\) below the rim plane, and \(y\) outside, at depth \(b=z_L-z_y>0\). Reflect \(y\) in the rim plane to \(\tilde y\). Every route through the plane is as long as the corresponding route to \(\tilde y\), and the shortest of those is the straight segment from \(x\) to \(\tilde y\). The two vectors \(x-\tilde y\) and \(x-y\) have the same horizontal part, and vertical parts \(-(a+b)\) and \(-(a-b)\), so

$$\delta(x,y)^2=\|x-y\|^2+(a+b)^2-(a-b)^2=\|x-y\|^2+4ab .$$

If \(y\) lies above the rim plane, the straight line already passes through the plane and \(\delta=\|x-y\|\). Averaging these squared point distances over the spoon's samples, exactly as the chord was averaged above, changes the squared distance between two scenes only through the samples that are inside the cup in one scene and outside it in the other. For every scene, record for each sample \(k\) its depth \(A_k\) below the rim if it is in the cup and zero otherwise, and its depth \(B_k\) below the rim plane if it is outside and below that plane, and zero otherwise. Over \(K_c\) samples the correction to the squared distance between scenes \(i\) and \(j\) is

$$\Delta_{ij}=\frac{4}{K_c}\bigl(A^{(i)}\cdot B^{(j)}+A^{(j)}\cdot B^{(i)}\bigr).$$

One matrix product over the scenes that have material in the cup gives every \(\Delta_{ij}\) at once. The result is still a metric: gluing the inside of the cup to the outside along the plane of the rim, with straight-line distance in each piece, satisfies the triangle inequality, and it lies between the chord and the true shortest motion. It changes the kernel only where material crosses the opening, and there it adds the extra length that the wall forces on that material.

5. Defining the objective function and scoring a scene

We can now measure how far a release carries its starting scene: it is \(d(s,e(s))\). A scene at rest stays where it is, so this is zero there, and it grows with the size of the motion. If the release takes a scene to a resting scene \(s^\star\), it equals the distance from the scene to the rest that the physics assigns it, so within the region of scenes that all fall to the same rest, the objective is a distance to that rest.

Two further terms complete the objective. The first keeps the placements clean: a starting overlap beyond the contact tolerance of 0.16 mm is charged with a weight \(\eta\). The second concerns contact. A spoon lying on the table well away from the mug is also at rest, and such scenes would otherwise be minima like any other. They are not what we are looking for, and in earlier runs they absorbed a large share of the particles. We therefore charge the gap between the bodies at the end of the release, beyond the contact tolerance of 1 mm. With \((a)_+=\max(a,0)\), the objective of particle \(x\) is

$$F(x)=d\bigl(s,e(s)\bigr)+\eta\bigl(\delta_0(s)-0.16\ \text{mm}\bigr)_++\bigl(g(e(s))-1\ \text{mm}\bigr)_+,\qquad s=T(x),$$

where \(g\) is the distance between the two bodies and \(\eta=18.0\). Each millimetre of excess starting overlap costs \(\eta\) millimetres; each millimetre of gap beyond 1 mm costs one. A resting scene in which the bodies touch keeps its objective unchanged, so every touching minimum stays a minimum; a resting scene in which they are apart now costs its gap, so it is no longer a minimum. For example, a spoon lying at rest 5 mm from the mug now has the objective 4 mm. No gate, rejection or label is involved: the term is part of the scalar objective, and the consensus weights of Section 2 see it like any other part.

The gap needs care. A general-purpose distance routine between the convex pieces of the two bodies proved unreliable near contact: moving the spoon by \(10^{-7}\) m could change it by tens of millimetres, and it reported contact for some pairs that were centimetres apart. The gap \(g\) used here is computed instead from the exact signed distance functions of the primitives, evaluated on the other body's surface samples: at 1 mm spacing near contact, and at 3 mm spacing over all pairs. It is stable to below a micrometre under the same small moves.

The objective tells particles which scenes to favour. A second score says whether a scene passes the finite rest test. It uses the maximum excursions, so motion that reverses before the end still counts. Each body's excursion beyond the tolerance \(\varepsilon=1\) mm contributes, in units of \(L=100\) mm, and the overlaps contribute the same charge as in the objective, now including the largest overlap during the release beyond 0.4 mm:

$$C=\sum_b\frac{(X_b-\varepsilon)_+}{L}+\frac{\eta}{L}\Bigl[(\delta-0.4\ \text{mm})_++(\delta_0-0.16\ \text{mm})_+\Bigr].$$

Every contribution is nonnegative, so \(C=0\) precisely when both bodies move by at most 1 mm and both overlap limits are met. A positive value measures the excess; for example, a spoon excursion of 3 mm with everything else within tolerance gives \(C=0.02\). A scene is called static when, in addition, it stays within the same excursion tolerance in ten-second releases at both 2 ms and 1 ms time steps, without the viscous drag, and quiet when its late speed is also below 1 mm/s. These remain finite numerical tests.

6. Contact types

The objective treats all resting scenes alike, whatever touches what. To see how a population of particles is spread over the families, we classify scenes by the kind of contact in them.

A contact type is read off a scene; we apply it to the end scene \(e(s)\) of a release. The mug's posture is upright, upside down, on its side or tilted, according to the vertical component of its axis (above 0.9, below \(-0.9\), within \(\pm0.3\), or in between). The spoon's relation to the mug is the first of these that applies: its bowl is inside the cup; only its handle tip is inside the cup; it touches the mug with its foot on the table and its shaft steeper than 15° (leaning) or flatter (against); it touches the mug without reaching the table, steep (propped) or flat (resting); or it does not touch the mug at all. That gives 28 coarse types, 24 of them with the bodies touching. A finer classification also records which parts touch, the spoon's bowl or handle against the mug's base, wall or handle, and whether the bowl faces up, down or sideways; it splits each touching coarse type into at most 18 fine types. Everything is computed from the release and from the gap \(g\) of Section 5, with its 1 mm contact tolerance.

7. Choosing a polarised consensus point

We now apply the consensus of Section 2 to a population of \(N\) particle states \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) in \(\mathcal X\). Each has a scene \(s_j=T(x_j)\), a released endpoint \(e(s_j)\) and an objective value \(F_j\) from Section 5. A particle is attracted towards a weighted mean of the others, and to choose the weights it needs to know how well another scene scores and how close it is.

Closeness is measured on both the starting scenes and the endpoints. Two placements can start close together but release into different scenes, and distant placements can end in the same place; a particle should follow another only if both are near. With the wall correction of Section 4 on each half,

$$D_{ij}^2=d(s_i,s_j)^2+d\bigl(e(s_i),e(s_j)\bigr)^2+\Delta_{ij}^{\text{start}}+\Delta_{ij}^{\text{end}}.$$

If two particles' releases end in different resting scenes, \(D_{ij}\) is at least the distance between those scenes, so a particle in the cup follows only particles whose releases also end in the cup or very near it.

The affinity is the one of Section 2, with \(D_{ij}\) in place of the Euclidean distance and \(\theta=0.1\) m. The weights are

$$w_{ij}=\exp\!\Bigl(-\alpha_i\bigl[F_j(F_i+\theta)+D_{ij}^2\bigr]\Bigr).$$

It remains to choose how sharply \(\alpha_i\) favours the smaller affinities. A large \(\alpha_i\) concentrates the weight on the few best and nearest sources; a small one spreads it over many. A convenient measure of the spread is the effective sample size,

$$\mathrm{ESS}_i=\frac{\bigl(\sum_jw_{ij}\bigr)^2}{\sum_jw_{ij}^2}.$$

It equals \(n\) when \(n\) sources carry equal weight and the others none, and it decreases continuously from \(N\) to 1 as \(\alpha_i\) grows from zero. So we can fix the number of sources we want each consensus point to combine and solve for \(\alpha_i\), by bisection in \(\log\alpha_i\). We ask for three, or for fewer when fewer particles lie within the particle's reach \(\rho_i=\sqrt{(F_i+\theta)F_i}\) of Section 2:

$$\mathrm{ESS}_i(\alpha_i)=\min(n_i,3),\qquad n_i=\#\{j:\ D_{ij}\le\rho_i\}.$$

The bisection is bounded above by \(\alpha_{\max}=1/(2\ell^2)\) with \(\ell=0.16\) mm, the contact-resolution scale, which corresponds to a Gaussian kernel of that width; in this run the solved values lie two to three orders of magnitude below it. A target of three keeps the consensus local. The number of sources a consensus point combines does not grow with the population, so additional particles narrow the kernel rather than averaging over more of the landscape. The target is fixed for the whole run, without annealing.

One more safeguard is needed. When a particle is much better than everything near it, the solved \(\alpha_i\) puts almost all the weight on the particle itself, and its consensus point coincides with it. The drift then vanishes and only the noise floor moves it. We cap the particle's own share of its weight at one half: if \(w_{ii}/\sum_jw_{ij}\gt\frac12\) at the solved \(\alpha_i\), \(\alpha_i\) is lowered to the largest value at which the own share is at most \(\frac12\). Because the own share decreases as \(\alpha_i\) decreases, this value is again found by bisection. Each consensus point then combines the particle with at least as much weight from its neighbours.

A term for crowded contact types

Consensus has a known weakness when families differ greatly in size. A family whose resting scenes fill a large region attracts many particles; a family whose scenes are rare, such as the spoon standing in the cup, holds only a few. The few are surrounded by members of larger families, the consensus averages over that surrounding, and the small family is drained one particle at a time. A remedy is to look at which contact type of Section 6 each particle's release ends in, and to favour the rare types.

Write \(n_k\) for the number of particles whose release ends in coarse type \(k\), and \(p_k=n_k/N\) for its share. Spreading the population evenly over the types means making the entropy \(-\sum_kp_k\log p_k\) large.

The first variation of the negative entropy with respect to the mass at a particle of type \(k\) is \(\log p_k+1\). Adding a multiple of it to the score makes particles of crowded types less attractive as sources and particles of rare types more so. Up to a constant, which does not change the weights,

$$\tilde F_j=F_j+w_0\,\log\frac{n_{k(j)}}{n_{\min}},$$

where \(k(j)\) is particle \(j\)'s type and \(n_{\min}\) the smallest count among the types present, so the added term is zero for the rarest type and positive for the others. The strength \(w_0\) is set at every update by asking how much the term changes the weights. In the exponent of \(w_{ij}\), the added term appears as \(\beta_j\,w_0\log(n_{k(j)}/n_{\min})\) with \(\beta_j=\alpha_j(F_j+\theta)\) the particle's own selectivity, where \(\alpha_j\) is solved by the rule above with \(F\) alone. We choose \(w_0\) so that the median of this product, over the particles whose type is not the rarest, equals one: the term then changes the typical weight by a factor of \(e\). The weights then use \(\tilde F\) in place of \(F\), in the affinity and in the reach, and \(\alpha_i\) is solved by the same rule for these weights:

$$w_{ij}=\exp\!\Bigl(-\alpha_i\bigl[\tilde F_j(\tilde F_i+\theta)+D_{ij}^2\bigr]\Bigr).$$

This changes only the consensus, not the particle equation.

The consensus point

The consensus point itself is the minimiser of a weighted sum of squared distances, now taken factor by factor on \(\mathcal X\). For the order coordinate this is the ordinary weighted mean \(\bar p_i\). For the attitude, minimising \(\sum_jw_{ij}\|v-u_j\|^2\) over unit vectors \(v\) is the same as maximising \(v\cdot\sum_jw_{ij}u_j\), so

$$\bar u_i=\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}u_j}{\bigl\|\sum_jw_{ij}u_j\bigr\|}.$$

The offsets are averaged as vectors and the mean is brought back into the collar of \(\bar u_i\): projected onto the plane orthogonal to \(\bar u_i\), and scaled to the unit circle if it lies outside. For the spoon's rotation, minimising \(\sum_jw_{ij}\|M-R_j\|_F^2\) over \(M\in SO(3)\) gives the closest rotation to the weighted matrix mean,

$$\bar R_i=\operatorname{Proj}_{SO(3)}\!\left(\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}R_j}{\sum_jw_{ij}}\right),$$

computed from a singular value decomposition. Together these give the consensus point \(m_i=(\bar p_i,\bar u_i,\bar\xi_i,\bar R_i)\). These are chordal means; the affinity compares physical scenes and their releases, while the averaging takes place factor by factor in the particle coordinates. It is not a claim that the consensus point's own scene is at rest.

8. Births and deaths over contact types

The term of Section 7 acts only through the weights, and so only where the consensus can carry particles from one family to another. A second mechanism moves mass between types directly. In a Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao flow, a density changes by transport, as in the particle equation, and by a reaction in which mass is created where a fitness is low and removed where it is high. For the entropy over the fine contact types of Section 6, with \(n_k\) and \(p_k\) now counting fine types, the reaction part reads

$$\partial_t\rho=-\lambda_{\text{FR}}\bigl(\phi-\mathbb E_\rho\phi\bigr)\rho,\qquad\phi(x)=\log n_{k(x)}.$$

It conserves mass, because \(\int(\phi-\mathbb E_\rho\phi)\rho=0\). Summed over each type, it moves the shares as \(\dot p_k=-\lambda_{\text{FR}}(\log p_k-\bar\phi)p_k\) with \(\bar\phi=\sum_lp_l\log p_l\) (the constant \(\log N\) cancels), and the entropy then grows at the rate

$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(-\sum_kp_k\log p_k\Bigr)=-\sum_k(\log p_k+1)\,\dot p_k=\lambda_{\text{FR}}\sum_kp_k(\log p_k-\bar\phi)^2\ \ge\ 0,$$

the variance of \(\log p\) under the shares. The rate is fastest when the shares are most uneven, and it stops only when all types present are equally populated. Crucially, the reaction moves mass between types without moving it through the landscape, so it does not have to wait for the consensus to carry particles across the space between families.

With a finite population and \(N\) fixed, the reaction becomes a jump process applied once per update, right after the evaluation and before the consensus. Each particle whose type is over-represented, \(\phi_i\gt\bar\phi\) (now the particle average of \(\phi\)), dies with probability \(\min\bigl(1,c(\phi_i-\bar\phi)\bigr)\), except that no type loses its last particle. Every death is replaced by a copy of a particle \(j\) of an under-represented type, drawn with probability proportional to \(\bar\phi-\phi_j\). The copy takes its parent's whole state, scene and evaluation, and the noise of the next step separates it from its parent. To see that this is the reaction in expectation, note that \(\sum_i(\phi_i-\bar\phi)=0\), so the positive and negative parts have the same sum \(\Sigma\). When no death probability is clipped at one, the expected number of deaths is \(c\Sigma\), and a type \(k\) with \(\phi_k\lt\bar\phi\) expects

$$c\Sigma\cdot\frac{n_k(\bar\phi-\phi_k)}{\Sigma}=c\,n_k(\bar\phi-\phi_k)$$

births, while a type with \(\phi_k\gt\bar\phi\) expects \(c\,n_k(\phi_k-\bar\phi)\) deaths. Either way the expected change is \(-c\,n_k(\phi_k-\bar\phi)\), which is the reaction with \(\lambda_{\text{FR}}\Delta t=c\). The constant \(c\) is fixed at update 0 so that 1 % of the particles are expected to die there, which gives \(c=0.0122\), and as the shares even out the number of jumps falls by itself. The jumps draw from their own random generator, so the particle equation's noise is unchanged.

9. Deriving the anisotropic diffusion

The particle equation of Section 2 adds the same noise to every coordinate. Before using it, we should ask what equal steps in our coordinates do to the bodies. Rotations are measured in radians and the offset in units of \(L=0.1\) m. Turning the spoon about its own shaft by one radian moves its surface points by 5.74 mm in root mean square, because they lie close to the shaft; tipping the shaft by one radian moves them by 57.55 mm, 10.02 times as much. Isotropic noise nevertheless gives the turn about the shaft the same variance as every other coordinate, so part of its effort goes into a motion that barely changes the scene.

We would like noise that, step for step, moves the material of the two bodies by comparable amounts in every direction. To build it, we first describe how a small change of each coordinate moves the two bodies, then measure how much material that motion displaces, and from this obtain a metric on the coordinates that shapes the noise.

9.1 How each coordinate moves the bodies

Write a small change of the seven geometric coordinates as \(\delta y=(\delta y_u,\delta y_w,\delta y_R)\): a tangent step \(\delta y_u\) of the attitude in a basis \(e_1,e_2\) of the plane orthogonal to \(u\), a change \(\delta y_w\) of the offset \(w\) in the same basis and in units of \(L\), and a turn \(\delta y_R\) of the spoon about its own axes. The order coordinate moves no material and is left aside. Each step moves each body rigidly, so it is described by the body's twist: the velocity \(V\) of its centre of mass, in units of \(L\), and its angular velocity \(\Omega\).

The offset and the spoon's turn are simple. A step along \(e_j\) in \(\delta y_w\) moves only the spoon's centre of mass, horizontally, by \(L\,R_{\text{mug}}e_j\). A step along \(e_j\) in \(\delta y_R\) turns only the spoon about its centre of mass, with world angular velocity \(R_{\text{spoon}}e_j\).

The attitude needs more care, because changing \(u\) with \(R\) held fixed carries the spoon with the mug. Let \(u(\varepsilon)\) move along the great circle in direction \(e_j\), and let the offset be carried into the new plane with its length kept, so that \(w(\varepsilon)=w-\varepsilon(w\cdot e_j)\,u+O(\varepsilon^2)\). The mug's world rotation \(S(u)\) changes with some angular velocity \(\Omega\). Differentiating its defining property \(S(u)\,u=-e_z\) gives \(\Omega\times(-e_z)+R_{\text{mug}}e_j=0\), that is

$$\Omega\times e_z=R_{\text{mug}}e_j .$$

This fixes the horizontal part of \(\Omega\) to \(\tau_j=e_z\times R_{\text{mug}}e_j\) and leaves its vertical part \(\psi\) free; a turn about the vertical is a gauge motion. Both bodies turn with \(\Omega\), because \(R_{\text{spoon}}=S(u)R\) with \(R\) fixed. The spoon's centre of mass, at \(W=R_{\text{mug}}w\) from the mug's, moves by

$$\frac{dW}{d\varepsilon}=\Omega\times W+R_{\text{mug}}\frac{dw}{d\varepsilon}=\tau_j\times W+\psi\,e_z\times W+(w\cdot e_j)\,e_z ,$$

using \(R_{\text{mug}}u=-e_z\). The first term is vertical, since \(\tau_j\) and \(W\) are both horizontal, and equals \(e_z\,[e_z\cdot(\tau_j\times W)]\). The last term cancels it exactly, because

$$w\cdot e_j=W\cdot R_{\text{mug}}e_j=W\cdot(\tau_j\times e_z)=-e_z\cdot(\tau_j\times W).$$

What remains, \(\psi\,e_z\times W\) together with the turn \(\psi e_z\) of both bodies, is a rigid turn of the whole scene about the vertical through the mug's centre of mass, a gauge motion. So, apart from the gauge, tilting the attitude turns both bodies by \(\tau_j\), each about its own centre of mass, and moves neither centre. These twists agree with finite differences of the solver's map to \(8\times10^{-10}\).

Besides these seven motions, the table gauge \(\Gamma\) of Section 1.1 moves the scene in three ways of its own: the two horizontal translations of the whole scene, and its turn about the vertical through the mug's centre of mass. They change neither the objective nor the physics. Numbering the ten motions \(\alpha=1,\ldots,10\), the seven coordinate directions followed by the three gauge motions, their twists are

$$\begin{array}{l|cc|cc} \text{motion }\alpha & V_{\text{mug}}^\alpha & \Omega_{\text{mug}}^\alpha & V_{\text{spoon}}^\alpha & \Omega_{\text{spoon}}^\alpha\\ \hline \text{attitude along }e_j,\ j=1,2 & 0 & \tau_j & 0 & \tau_j\\ \text{offset along }e_j,\ j=1,2 & 0 & 0 & R_{\text{mug}}e_j & 0\\ \text{spoon turn about its axis }e_j,\ j=1,2,3 & 0 & 0 & 0 & R_{\text{spoon}}e_j\\ \text{shift of the scene along }e_x\text{ or }e_y & e_x\text{ or }e_y & 0 & e_x\text{ or }e_y & 0\\ \text{turn of the scene about the mug's vertical} & 0 & e_z & e_z\times W & e_z \end{array}$$

with \(W\) in units of \(L\). We collect them as the columns of a \(12\times10\) matrix \(C\), column \(\alpha\) being \((V_{\text{mug}}^\alpha,\Omega_{\text{mug}}^\alpha,V_{\text{spoon}}^\alpha,\Omega_{\text{spoon}}^\alpha)\). A combination \(c\in\mathbb R^{10}\) of the ten motions gives the two bodies the twists \(Cc\).

9.2 The mean squared displacement of a moving body

We measure a motion by the mean squared displacement of the bodies' surface samples, the same convention as the embedding \(\Psi\) of Section 4. Take one body, with centre of mass \(c\) and surface samples \(q_1,\ldots,q_n\) in the body's own frame, measured from \(c\) in units of \(L\). The samples are spread uniformly by area, so each stands for the same area and counts equally: \(n=131\,072\) on the mug and \(n=32\,768\) on the spoon. When the body has rotation \(R\), sample \(k\) sits at

$$x_k=c+r_k,\qquad r_k=R\,q_k .$$

In a rigid motion \(c\) and \(R\) change with time and the samples \(q_k\) do not, so

$$\dot x_k=\dot c+\dot R\,q_k .$$

Differentiating \(R^\top R=I_3\) gives \(\dot R^\top R+R^\top\dot R=0\), so the matrix \(\dot RR^\top\) is skew-symmetric. A skew-symmetric \(3\times3\) matrix is the cross-product matrix \([\Omega]_\times\) of a vector, \([\Omega]_\times x=\Omega\times x\), and this \(\Omega\) is the body's angular velocity in world coordinates. With \(V=\dot c\) and \(R^\top R=I_3\),

$$\dot x_k=V+\dot R\,R^\top R\,q_k=V+[\Omega]_\times\,r_k=V+\Omega\times r_k .$$

For a velocity \(\delta y\) of the coordinates, \(V\) and \(\Omega\) are the twist of Section 9.1 and \(V+\Omega\times r_k\) is the velocity of sample \(k\). Its squared length expands as

$$\|V+\Omega\times r_k\|^2=\|V\|^2+2\,V\cdot(\Omega\times r_k)+\|\Omega\times r_k\|^2 ,$$

and Lagrange's identity \(\|a\times b\|^2=\|a\|^2\|b\|^2-(a\cdot b)^2\) turns the last term into a quadratic form in \(\Omega\):

$$\|\Omega\times r_k\|^2=\|\Omega\|^2\|r_k\|^2-(\Omega\cdot r_k)^2=\Omega^\top\bigl(\|r_k\|^2I_3-r_kr_k^\top\bigr)\,\Omega .$$

Now average over the samples. The first term does not depend on \(k\); the second is linear in \(r_k\), so the average moves inside the cross product; the third has a matrix that is linear in the sample terms:

$$\frac1n\sum_k\|V\|^2=\|V\|^2,\qquad \frac1n\sum_k2\,V\cdot(\Omega\times r_k)=2\,V\cdot\Bigl(\Omega\times\frac1n\sum_kr_k\Bigr),$$ $$\frac1n\sum_k\Omega^\top\bigl(\|r_k\|^2I_3-r_kr_k^\top\bigr)\,\Omega=\Omega^\top\Bigl[\frac1n\sum_k\bigl(\|r_k\|^2I_3-r_kr_k^\top\bigr)\Bigr]\,\Omega .$$

Collecting the three terms,

$$\frac1n\sum_k\|V+\Omega\times r_k\|^2=\|V\|^2+2\,V\cdot(\Omega\times s)+\Omega^\top I\,\Omega,\qquad s=\frac1n\sum_kr_k,\qquad I=\frac1n\sum_k\bigl(\|r_k\|^2I_3-r_kr_k^\top\bigr).$$

Every step is an identity. The vector \(s\) is the centroid of the samples relative to the centre of mass, which does not vanish because the centroid of a surface is not the centre of mass, and \(I\) is the inertia tensor of the samples, each of mass \(1/n\). Since \(r_k=Rq_k\) and \(\|r_k\|=\|q_k\|\), both rotate with the body,

$$s=R\,s_0,\qquad I=R\,I_0\,R^\top,\qquad s_0=\frac1n\sum_kq_k,\qquad I_0=\frac1n\sum_k\bigl(\|q_k\|^2I_3-q_kq_k^\top\bigr),$$

so the samples of a body reduce to the vector \(s_0\) and the \(3\times3\) matrix \(I_0\), computed once in its own frame. Finally, the cross term can be written \(2\,V\cdot(\Omega\times s)=-2\,V^\top[s]_\times\Omega=V^\top(-[s]_\times)\,\Omega+\Omega^\top[s]_\times V\), using \([s]_\times^\top=-[s]_\times\), so the whole form is one \(6\times6\) matrix acting on the twist:

$$\frac1n\sum_k\|V+\Omega\times r_k\|^2=\begin{pmatrix}V\\ \Omega\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}K\begin{pmatrix}V\\ \Omega\end{pmatrix},\qquad K=\begin{pmatrix}I_3&-[s]_\times\\ [s]_\times&I\end{pmatrix}.$$

9.3 The material metric

Write \(K_{\text{mug}}\) and \(K_{\text{spoon}}\) for the matrices of the two bodies. By Section 9.2, a combination \(c\in\mathbb R^{10}\) of the ten motions of Section 9.1, which gives the bodies the twists \(Cc\), moves their samples by the mean squared displacement \(c^\top\mathcal M\,c\), summed over the two bodies, with

$$\mathcal M=C^\top\begin{pmatrix}K_{\text{mug}}&0\\ 0&K_{\text{spoon}}\end{pmatrix}C,\qquad \mathcal M_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{b\in\{\text{mug},\,\text{spoon}\}}\begin{pmatrix}V_b^\alpha\\ \Omega_b^\alpha\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}K_b\begin{pmatrix}V_b^\beta\\ \Omega_b^\beta\end{pmatrix}.$$

The diagonal entry \(\mathcal M_{\alpha\alpha}\) is the mean squared displacement of motion \(\alpha\) alone. We split \(\mathcal M\) into the seven coordinate rows and the three gauge rows,

$$\mathcal M=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal M_{yy}&\mathcal M_{yg}\\ \mathcal M_{gy}&\mathcal M_{gg}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathcal M_{yy}\in\mathbb R^{7\times7},\quad \mathcal M_{yg}=\mathcal M_{gy}^\top\in\mathbb R^{7\times3},\quad \mathcal M_{gg}\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}.$$

A coordinate change \(\delta y\) and the same change followed by a gauge motion \(g\in\mathbb R^3\) describe the same change of the scene, so a displacement and the same displacement plus a gauge motion must count as one. We therefore measure \(\delta y\) by the smallest displacement over all gauge corrections:

$$\delta y^\top G\,\delta y=\min_{g\in\mathbb R^3}q(g),\qquad q(g)=\begin{pmatrix}\delta y\\ g\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\mathcal M\begin{pmatrix}\delta y\\ g\end{pmatrix}=\delta y^\top\mathcal M_{yy}\,\delta y+2\,g^\top\mathcal M_{gy}\,\delta y+g^\top\mathcal M_{gg}\,g .$$

Every gauge motion moves the samples, so \(\mathcal M_{gg}\) is positive definite and \(q\) is a convex quadratic in \(g\). Its minimum is where the gradient vanishes,

$$\nabla_gq=2\,\mathcal M_{gy}\,\delta y+2\,\mathcal M_{gg}\,g=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g^\star=-\mathcal M_{gg}^{-1}\mathcal M_{gy}\,\delta y ,$$

and substituting \(g^\star\) into \(q\),

$$\delta y^\top G\,\delta y=\delta y^\top\mathcal M_{yy}\,\delta y-2\,\delta y^\top\mathcal M_{yg}\mathcal M_{gg}^{-1}\mathcal M_{gy}\,\delta y+\delta y^\top\mathcal M_{yg}\mathcal M_{gg}^{-1}\mathcal M_{gy}\,\delta y,\qquad G=\mathcal M_{yy}-\mathcal M_{yg}\,\mathcal M_{gg}^{-1}\,\mathcal M_{gy}.$$

This symmetric \(7\times7\) matrix is the material metric; it depends on the particle's state. Because any two ways of building the world scene from the particle differ by a gauge motion, which the minimum absorbs, \(G\) does not depend on the choice of the section \(S(u)\).

\(G\) is measured in \(L^2\) per unit coordinate squared. To work in a unit that does not depend on the state, let \(\mu_0\) be the uniform law on \(\mathcal X\), in which \(u\) is uniform on the sphere, \(\xi\) uniform in area on its disc and \(R\) uniform on \(SO(3)\), and divide by the average diagonal entry of \(G\) under it:

$$\bar c=\tfrac17\,\mathbb E_{\mu_0}\bigl[\operatorname{tr}G\bigr],\qquad \tilde G=\frac{G}{\bar c}.$$

A Monte Carlo average over 200 000 draws of \(\mu_0\) gives \(\bar c=0.31384\,L^2\), with standard error \(4.1\times10^{-5}\,L^2\).

The lowering is not part of this metric. The first body's height is the support function of its shape in the downward direction, which has a corner at every resting posture on a flat face and jumps whenever the supporting point changes; a metric including it would not be smooth exactly where it matters. Without the lowering, \(G\) is a polynomial in the entries of the rotations and the offset, smooth everywhere.

9.4 What the metric says

Write the eigen-decomposition of \(\tilde G\) as

$$\tilde G\,v_k=\lambda_k\,v_k,\qquad |v_k|=1,\qquad \lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_7 .$$

A unit step of the coordinates along \(v_k\) moves the material by the mean square \(v_k^\top Gv_k=\bar c\,\lambda_k\), so the eigen-directions show where the coordinates are cheap and where they are dear. On the particles of the run at update 372, the medians of the eigenvalues are 0.0103, 0.272, 0.313, 0.664, 1.49, 1.61, 2.49; the largest median is 241.1 times the smallest. Reading off the world motion of each eigen-direction, per unit of the coordinates:

eigenvalue of \(\tilde G\)what the bodies do
0.010the spoon turns about its own shaft (0.98 rad per unit), while the mug barely moves (0.02 rad)
0.27the mug tilts in the world (0.60 rad) while the spoon turns back about a transverse axis by about a third as much (0.21 rad, opposite sense)
0.31the same kind of motion about the other horizontal axis (mug 0.60 rad, spoon 0.27 rad back)
0.66the mug tilts (1.00 rad) and carries the spoon, which only rolls about its shaft (1.01 rad, same sense)
1.49the spoon's centre of mass moves relative to the mug's (0.86 L) while the spoon tips its shaft (0.55 rad)
1.61the offset alone: the spoon's centre of mass moves relative to the mug's (0.99 L)
2.49the mug tilts (0.80 rad) and carries the spoon so that its shaft tips, and the spoon turns further in the same sense (1.40 rad)

The coupling of the relative coordinates, in which tilting the mug carries the spoon, thus appears in the metric at its material cost: cheap when the carried spoon only rolls, dear when it tips.

9.5 Noise shaped by the metric

Now shape the noise of the seven geometric coordinates by the inverse metric. Take the increment

$$\eta=a\,\tilde G^{-1/2}z,\qquad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_7),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\eta)=a^2\,\tilde G^{-1},$$

where \(\tilde G^{-1/2}\) is any square root of \(\tilde G^{-1}\); the solver uses the inverse transpose of the Cholesky factor of \(\tilde G\), which gives the same covariance. Along \(v_k\), the spread of the coordinates is \(\mathbb E[(v_k\cdot\eta)^2]=a^2\,v_k^\top\tilde G^{-1}v_k=a^2/\lambda_k\), and the squared material displacement is \(\bar c\lambda_k\) times that:

$$\bar c\,\lambda_k\;\mathbb E\bigl[(v_k\cdot\eta)^2\bigr]=\bar c\,\lambda_k\,\frac{a^2}{\lambda_k}=a^2\,\bar c\qquad\text{for every }k.$$

Isotropic noise of the same amplitude, \(\eta=a\,z\), has \(\mathbb E[(v_k\cdot\eta)^2]=a^2\) and gives direction \(k\) the squared material displacement \(a^2\bar c\,\lambda_k\). In total, the shaped noise moves the material by

$$\mathbb E\bigl[\eta^\top G\,\eta\bigr]=a^2\operatorname{tr}\bigl(G\,\tilde G^{-1}\bigr)=a^2\bar c\operatorname{tr}I_7=7\,a^2\bar c$$

at every state, while the isotropic noise moves it by \(a^2\operatorname{tr}G=a^2\bar c\operatorname{tr}\tilde G\), which changes from state to state and whose average over \(\mu_0\) is \(7a^2\bar c\) by the definition of \(\bar c\). The isotropic noise puts \(\lambda_7/\lambda_1\) times more into the stiffest direction than into the softest, 241.1 at the median eigenvalues; the shaped noise puts the same into each.

9.6 The amplitude must be measured in the same metric

Reshaping the noise alone is not enough. The amplitude of Section 2 is \(a=\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,(|D|+\kappa)\), where \(D=(D_p,D_y)\) is the particle's displacement from its consensus point in the order coordinate and the seven geometric coordinates, and \(|D|^2=D_p^2+|D_y|^2\). Hold the consensus point fixed and take one step of the attraction and the noise, \(D'=(1-\Delta t)D+\zeta\), where the noise \(\zeta\) of the eight coordinates has mean zero and covariance \(a^2\Sigma\). The cross term has mean zero, so

$$\mathbb E|D'|^2=(1-\Delta t)^2|D|^2+\mathbb E|\zeta|^2=(1-\Delta t)^2|D|^2+\Delta t\,\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}\Sigma\,\bigl(|D|+\kappa\bigr)^2 .$$

For isotropic noise \(\Sigma=I_8\), and with \(\kappa=0\) the factor in front of \(|D|^2\) is \((1-\Delta t)^2+8\Delta t\,\sigma^2\). It is below one, so that a particle approaches its consensus point, when \(\sigma^2\lt(2-\Delta t)/8\), that is \(\sigma\lt0.487\) at \(\Delta t=0.1\). The run uses 95 % of this bound, \(\sigma=0.463\): as much noise as the attraction can still absorb, so that particles explore as widely as convergence allows.

With the shaped noise and the same coordinate distance, however, \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,\tilde G^{-1})\) and

$$\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=1+\sum_k\frac1{\lambda_k},$$

which is 107.87 at the median eigenvalues, 96.79 of it from the shaft roll alone. At the same \(\sigma\) the factor becomes 3.122: a displacement along the roll grows, a larger displacement gives a larger amplitude in every direction, and the particle heats up instead of converging.

The remedy is to measure the distance in the metric that shapes the noise. Let \(\bar G=\operatorname{diag}(1,\tilde G)\) act on the order and geometric parts of the displacement, and set

$$|D|_{\bar G}^2=D^\top\bar G\,D=D_p^2+D_y^\top\tilde G\,D_y,\qquad a=\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\bigl(|D|_{\bar G}+\kappa\bigr).$$

Repeating the computation in the norm of \(\bar G\), with \(\zeta\) of covariance \(a^2\bar G^{-1}\) and therefore \(\mathbb E|\zeta|^2_{\bar G}=a^2\operatorname{tr}(\bar G\,\bar G^{-1})=8a^2\),

$$\mathbb E|D'|^2_{\bar G}=(1-\Delta t)^2|D|^2_{\bar G}+8\,\Delta t\,\sigma^2\,\bigl(|D|_{\bar G}+\kappa\bigr)^2,$$

which is the contraction of the isotropic model, now measured in the material norm. Where \(\tilde G\) is the identity, the shaped noise is the isotropic one. Measured in \(\bar G\), a displacement along \(v_k\) has \(\sqrt{\lambda_k}\) times its length in the coordinates: 0.102 for the shaft roll and 1.578 for the stiffest direction at the median eigenvalues.

9.7 The drift that fixes which diffusion is meant

A noise whose covariance changes from place to place is not yet a well-defined diffusion: the same covariance field, written in different coordinates, implies different drifts, so a drift term must say which diffusion is meant. Since the amplitude factor \(a^2\) is kept in Itô form, as in the reference model, the drift is \(a^2b\) with \(b\) built from \(\tilde G\) alone. Two choices are natural:

$$b^j_{\text{LB}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{|\tilde G|}}\,\partial_i\Bigl(\sqrt{|\tilde G|}\,\tilde G^{ij}\Bigr),\qquad\qquad b^j=\frac{1}{2\rho}\,\partial_i\bigl(\rho\,\tilde G^{ij}\bigr).$$

The first, the Laplace–Beltrami drift, gives the Brownian motion of the metric itself, whose invariant law is the metric's volume, with density \(\sqrt{|\tilde G|}\). The second, the reference-measure drift, keeps a chosen law invariant: its generator

$$\mathcal Lf=\frac{a^2}{2}\,\rho^{-1}\,\partial_i\bigl(\rho\,\tilde G^{ij}\,\partial_jf\bigr)$$

is symmetric with respect to the law with density \(\rho\), and leaves that law invariant. We choose for \(\rho\) the density of the law that the isotropic noise of the reference model leaves invariant, so that the shaped noise changes only the local directions and speeds of the noise, not where pure noise would send the particles. The Laplace–Beltrami drift would instead favour configurations of larger material volume.

That law is not the starting law \(\mu_0\). The isotropic noise turns the attitude and the spoon by geodesic steps and moves the offset by steps of the physical offset \(w=H(\xi/|\xi|)\,\xi\) in units of \(L\), so pure noise leaves invariant the law

$$\nu(du\,dw\,dR)=dA_{S^2}(u)\;d^2w\;dR,$$

area on the unit sphere for \(u\), area in the plane for \(w\) and the Haar measure for \(R\). Relative to \(\mu_0\), which is uniform in the area of \(\xi\), its density is proportional to \(H(\xi/|\xi|)^2\): a step of \(w\) is a step of \(\xi\) of size \(L/H\), slower where the collar is wide, and a diffusion without drift spends more time where it moves slowly.

To evaluate the drift, the solver uses coordinates centred at the particle: geodesic steps \(y_u\) of the attitude and \(y_R\) of the spoon's rotation, and steps \(y_w\) of the offset in units of \(L\), carried into the tilted plane with their length kept as in Section 9.1. In these coordinates \(\nu(dy)=\rho(y)\,dy\), with

$$\rho(y)\ \propto\ \underbrace{\frac{\sin|y_u|}{|y_u|}}_{\text{sphere}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\cos|y_u|}{1-\sin^2|y_u|\,\cos^2\varphi}}_{\text{offset}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{2\,(1-\cos|y_R|)}{|y_R|^2}}_{\text{rotation}},$$

where \(\varphi\) is the angle between the offset and the tilt direction \(y_u\). Each factor is the change of volume of one part of the coordinates.

The sphere. At the angle \(\theta=|y_u|\) from the particle's attitude, the sphere's area element is \(\sin\theta\,d\theta\) times the element of the azimuth, while the plane of \(y_u\) has \(\theta\,d\theta\) times the same; their ratio is \(\sin\theta/\theta\).

The offset. When the attitude tilts by \(\theta\), projection into the tilted plane shortens the offset's component along the tilt by \(\cos\theta\) and keeps the component across it; restoring the length leaves the radius unchanged and moves the polar angle from \(\varphi\) to \(\varphi'\), with

$$\tan\varphi'=\frac{\tan\varphi}{\cos\theta},\qquad \frac{d\varphi'}{d\varphi}=\frac{\cos\theta}{\cos^2\theta\cos^2\varphi+\sin^2\varphi}=\frac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta\,\cos^2\varphi}.$$

The area element \(r\,dr\,d\varphi\) of the plane becomes \(r\,dr\,d\varphi'\), so the area changes by this factor.

The rotation. A turn by the angle \(\vartheta\) about an axis has Haar density proportional to \(1-\cos\vartheta\) in the variables \((\vartheta,\text{axis})\), and \(dy_R=\vartheta^2\,d\vartheta\,d(\text{axis})\), which gives the last factor.

All three factors are even in \(y_u\) and in \(y_R\), and the middle one equals 1 for every offset when \(y_u=0\). Hence \(\partial_i\rho=0\) at the particle, \(y=0\), and expanding the drift,

$$b^j=\frac{1}{2\rho}\,\partial_i\bigl(\rho\,\tilde G^{ij}\bigr)=\frac12\,\partial_i\tilde G^{ij}+\frac12\,\tilde G^{ij}\,\partial_i\log\rho\ \overset{y=0}{=}\ \frac12\,\partial_i\tilde G^{ij}.$$

The solver evaluates it by central differences of the closed-form metric with step \(10^{-4}\) in each of the seven coordinates, fourteen further evaluations per particle.

9.8 A physical reading

The result has a physical interpretation. Let every surface sample of a body feel a drag force proportional to its velocity and its share of the surface, \(-c_d\,\dot x_k/n\): friction spread evenly over the surface, without interaction between samples. The rate of dissipation of a rigid motion is then \(c_d\) times the quadratic form of Section 9.2, so \(c_d K\) is the body's resistance. By the fluctuation–dissipation relation, the overdamped Brownian motion of the two bodies at a temperature \(\Theta\), with no forces, has diffusion tensor \(2\Theta\) times the inverse resistance, a stochastic drift given by the divergence of that inverse, and the uniform measure of positions and rotations as its invariant law, which in the gauge-free coordinates is \(\nu\). This dynamics commutes with the table gauge, and projecting it onto the gauge-free coordinates gives exactly the shaped noise with the reference-measure drift. The noise is the Brownian motion of the two rigid bodies under surface friction, at a temperature that the consensus factor \(a^2\) sets for each particle. It contains no contact forces, no gravity and no table: it is a search device with a physical shape, not a simulation.

10. Keeping exploration active

The strength of the noise was fixed in Section 9.6 at \(\sigma=0.463\), 95 % of the largest value for which a particle still approaches its consensus point. One constant remains, the floor \(\kappa\) of the amplitude.

The floor keeps a particle that sits on its consensus point moving, at amplitude \(\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\kappa\). If it were too large, particles at rest would be kicked out of their resting scenes; if it were too small, they would never test their neighbourhood. Its size was measured on resting scenes. Kicked once by a random step of the noise's shape, half of them leave rest when the kick has the amplitude \(a=T=0.0042\). We want a resting particle to accumulate a kick of that size only over 100 updates. Independent kicks add in quadrature, so the kick per update is \(T/\sqrt{100}\), and

$$\kappa=\frac{T}{10\,\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}=0.0028 .$$

A resting particle is then moved by about 0.04 mm and 0.02° per update.

11. The stochastic dynamics on the search space

We now have the consensus points, the shaped noise and the jumps, and can write the dynamics. Optimisation time is \(t\), distinct from the release time \(\tau\), and the attraction rate is one. On each factor, write the displacement of particle \(i\) towards its consensus point in local coordinates: \(D_p=p_i-\bar p_i\) for the order coordinate, \(\operatorname{Log}_{u_i}\bar u_i\in T_{u_i}S^2\) for the attitude (the tangent vector at \(u_i\) pointing along the great circle to \(\bar u_i\), with length the angle between them), \(P_{u_i}\bar\xi_i-\xi_i\) for the offset with \(P_{u_i}\) the projection onto the plane orthogonal to \(u_i\), and \(\omega_i=\log(R_i^\top\bar R_i)^\vee\) for the spoon's rotation, the axis-angle vector of the turn that takes \(R_i\) to \(\bar R_i\). In the basis \(e_1,e_2\) of the plane orthogonal to \(u_i\), the offset enters with its physical length \(H\) and in units of \(L\), so the seven geometric components of the displacement are

$$D_y=\Bigl(-\operatorname{Log}_{u_i}\bar u_i,\ \ \frac{H}{L}\bigl(\xi_i-P_{u_i}\bar\xi_i\bigr),\ \ -\omega_i\Bigr),\qquad |D|_{\bar G}^2=D_p^2+D_y^\top\tilde GD_y .$$

With independent standard Brownian motions \(B^0_i\in\mathbb R\) and \(B_i\in\mathbb R^7\), the amplitude \(a_i=\sigma(|D|_{\bar G}+\kappa)\) and the shaped increment \(d\eta_i=a_i\,\tilde G^{-1/2}dB_i+a_i^2b\,dt\), the particle equations are

$$\begin{aligned} \substack{\text{order}\\\mathbb R}:\quad dp_i&=-(p_i-\bar p_i)\,dt+a_i\,dB^0_i,\\[0.8em] \substack{\text{attitude}\\S^2}:\quad du_i&=\operatorname{Log}_{u_i}\bar u_i\,dt+d\eta_{i,1}e_1+d\eta_{i,2}e_2\qquad(\text{moved along great circles}),\\[0.8em] \substack{\text{offset}\\\bar D_{u_i}}:\quad d\xi_i&=\bigl(P_{u_i}\bar\xi_i-\xi_i\bigr)\,dt+\frac{L}{H}\bigl(d\eta_{i,3}e_1+d\eta_{i,4}e_2\bigr)\qquad(\text{kept in the plane of }u_i,\ \text{reflected at }\|\xi\|=1),\\[0.8em] \substack{\text{spoon}\\SO(3)}:\quad dR_i&=R_i\,\widehat{\omega_i}\,dt+R_i\,\widehat{d\eta_{i,5..7}}\qquad(\text{Itô form, kept on }SO(3)\text{ by the exponential}). \end{aligned}$$

Here \(\widehat v\) is the skew matrix of \(v\). The order coordinate stays outside the metric and keeps an isotropic noise; only its sign is used by \(T\).

Between updates the particles follow these equations; at each update the jump process of Section 8 replaces some particles by copies of others. For the distribution of the population, the two act together. If \(\mathcal L^*\) denotes the Fokker–Planck operator of the particle equations, which depends on the population through the consensus points, the density evolves as

$$\partial_t\rho=\mathcal L^*_\rho\,\rho-\lambda_{\text{FR}}\bigl(\phi-\mathbb E_\rho\phi\bigr)\rho,$$

the transport of polarised consensus plus the Fisher–Rao reaction over contact types. The equations above are local equations on the interiors of the coordinate domains. Their time discretisation, and the treatment of the disc boundary and of the rotation-log cut, are given in Appendix A.6.

12. Starting the population

The particles start from the uniform measure \(\mu_0\) of Section 9.3, without any information about how the bodies rest, and the order is decided by a fair coin. The mug's attitude \(u\) is uniform on the sphere and the spoon's relative rotation \(R\) is uniform on \(SO(3)\), so that both world orientations are uniform too. The offset \(\xi\) is uniform over the area of the disc, \(\xi=\sqrt{U}\,(\cos\vartheta\,e_1+\sin\vartheta\,e_2)\) with \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), \(\vartheta\) uniform on the circle and \(e_1,e_2\) a basis of the plane orthogonal to \(u\). There are 10 000 particles. No body is settled beforehand and no posture is supplied; everything the population knows about resting scenes it learns from its own releases.

13. Result 1 - The cost landscape

Both results come from one run on seed 11, stopped after 372 updates and read out from its saved state.

The dropdown below selects a subfamily, a posture of the mug together with a relation of the spoon. Each picture is then a slice through one scene of that subfamily which the run found and which is static for ten seconds, the calmest one. Two of the particle's coordinates are changed on a grid and all others are held; every grid point is turned into a scene by the map \(T\) and released exactly as a particle would be, and the height is its objective \(F\) in millimetres. The zeros of \(F\) are green: a square of the grid is green when all four of its corners are zeros, and any other zero is a green dot. The simulated release never returns a scene exactly where it started, so \(F\) never vanishes exactly (its smallest value on these slices is 0.13 mm), and a cell counts as a zero when \(F\) is at most the rest tolerance \(\varepsilon=1\) mm of Section 5. This is a tolerance on \(F\) itself, not the rest test: \(F\) compares where the release ends with where it began, while the rest test bounds how far any point moves on the way and how deeply the bodies overlap. Some zeros of \(F\) therefore fail the rest test, and a spoon at rest on the table apart from the mug passes it without being a zero, because the contact term charges its gap. Hovering over a cell shows both. Cells outside the collar are left empty. The dot marks the scene itself. Three pairs of coordinates are shown side by side: the spoon's offset, in two directions of the horizontal plane; the mug's attitude, tilted in two directions; and the spoon's rotation, turned about its two transverse axes. The close-up covers ±60 mm or ±60° around the scene. The whole range covers the entire collar disc, and turns of up to half a revolution. Dragging turns the three pictures together.

its components in the gallery ↓

The scene the slices go through, from the side and from above. Click to turn it.

Range Top of the height scale
zero of \(F\), that is \(F\le 1\) mm

Three things can be read off these surfaces. The first is that the objective is graded around every scene. Turning the spoon or the mug away from the scene by 1.5°, 3°, 6°, 12° and 24° raises it to 2.1, 4.3, 9, 20 and 47 mm at the median over the 17 subfamilies, the two bodies, the two axes and both senses. A particle some ten degrees away from a scene at rest is told which way to turn.

The second is that the zero set of \(F\) is wide for some subfamilies and thin for others. Averaged over the three close-up slices, the share of cells that are zeros is largest for upside down, resting (16 %) and upright, resting (15 %), and smallest for on its side, leaning (0.1 %) and on its side, bowl in (0.2 %). The thin ones are where a particle must land precisely, and where a consensus that averages over neighbours of other subfamilies would most easily pull it away.

The third is the cliffs. Over all close-up slices the median objective is 75 mm, but within a few degrees or millimetres of many scenes the surface jumps by tens of millimetres where the release changes destination, for example where the spoon falls off the rim or out of the cup. The surface beyond a cliff says nothing about the scene on the near side of it.

14. Result 2 - Stable scenes obtained, by component

A family name says what touches what, but it does not say whether two scenes with the same name can be turned into each other without passing through scenes that move. The question the gallery answers is that one. Two static scenes are joined when a sampled path of scenes between them stays static all the way: the two scenes are expressed with the same placement order, the mug's attitude, the spoon's rotation and the offset are interpolated in small steps (at most 1 mm and 0.5° nominally, with neighbouring samples within 2 mm in the material embedding), each intermediate pose is closed vertically onto contact, and every one of them must pass the solver's one-second rest test, the starting-overlap and contact limits, and both ten-second checks. Joined scenes are merged into groups, and the search for paths is repeated between the nearest scenes of different groups until no candidate pair remains under the declared rule.

The 6 585 consensus outcomes that are static for ten seconds fall into 230 such groups, joined by 6 609 successful paths; ten groups are single scenes. No group joins two contact types. A group is a numerical, path-tested component: a successful path joins its scenes, but failed or untested paths do not prove that two groups are separate, and the samples do not certify every point between them. Unfound curved paths can split one physical component into several groups.

The gallery is organised by the mug's posture, then by the spoon's relation to it, then by component. Choosing a subfamily here also selects its landscape in Section 13. Within a component, scenes closer than the chosen resolution (by default 5 mm or 3°, with the table gauge removed) to one already shown are left out. Each card gives the largest excursion of each body in the ten-second check; a click opens the scene to be turned.

15. What it does not do

It does not find every family. Of the 24 combinations of the mug's posture and a touching relation of the spoon, the run holds 17 with static scenes. Three of the others, the spoon propped steeply on an upside-down mug and the spoon propped or resting on a tilted mug, have no static scene in any earlier search of this mug and spoon, and a fourth, the spoon propped on an upright mug without its handle in the cup, only one; in this run their particles were all still falling when the release ended. The spoon inside a tilted mug, or with its handle there, has been seen static only in an earlier experiment in which the mug was placed at its tilted rest by hand, with the spoon pushed into an opening that faces down and sideways; the lowering of Section 1.5 can only place the spoon from above, so such scenes can be reached only by falling into them. Finally, the spoon on the table against a tilted mug is reached at every update but never comes to rest in this run: its particles keep an objective of 15 to 25 mm. With 50 000 particles it does come to rest (Appendix A.7).

It has been run once, on one seed, and stopped by request after 372 updates, when no new family had come to rest since update 165 and the spread of the population over types had stopped improving. At that point 1 386 of the 10 000 particles were at rest in the one-second release; the read-out of the consensus points was taken from the saved state.

The redistribution depends on contact types written for this pair of bodies: the posture bands of the mug, the parts of the spoon and the cavity of the cup. The births and deaths are a jump process added to the particle equation, not part of the consensus model itself, and they act on these labels. A version for other scenes would need types read from the contact graph alone, which parts of which bodies touch, and has not been built.

Its components are numerical path groups, not proved components, and several subfamilies are thin: mug on its side, spoon propped steeply (3); tilted mug, spoon leaning · foot on table (2); upright mug, spoon handle inside (2) have only two or three distinct static scenes each. The objective and the distance extend to more bodies by summing over them, and the collar can be built recursively, each body lowered onto the scene built before it. That does not establish scalable search: a release becomes more expensive as bodies and contacts are added, and the number of families can grow quickly. Nothing has been tested beyond two bodies.

Provenance: this is the birth–death run of the interaction-collar study of 16–17 November 2026 on seed 11, stopped by request before update 373; its consensus points were read out from the saved state of update 372 by the same evaluation without a further step.
