Appendix: results and numerical details

All numbers below are from the same run unless stated otherwise: seed 11, 10 000 particles, read out at update 372.

A.1 Particles at rest

particles at rest in the one-second release, of 10 000, against the update

The number of particles at rest in the one-second release rises to about a thousand by update 200 and then grows slowly, reaching 1 386 at update 372. The two runs without births and deaths hold more particles at rest at equal updates (1 865 with the type term only at update 350, 1 063 with the contact objective only at update 190), because births and deaths keep moving particles out of the crowded types and the copies start their descent again. At the read-out, 8 284 of the 10 000 consensus points are at rest in the one-second release, all of them in contact, and 6 585 pass the ten-second check.

The curve counts particles. The tiles, the gallery and the table of A.3 are taken on the consensus points of the last update, which are what a run returns and what the ten-second check is run on.

A.2 The spread of the population over contact types

effective number of contact types among particles in contact, against the update

The effective number of contact types, the exponential of the entropy of the shares of the particles in contact, measures how evenly the population is spread. With births and deaths it rises to 12.7 by update 200 and stays near 13.4; without them it settles near 4.1 with the type term only and 4.0 with the contact objective only. Particles in the rare relations (bowl in, handle in, leaning, propped, resting) number 5 463 at update 190 against 1 384 and 1 304. The run was stopped at update 372 because no new contact type had come to rest since update 165, the effective number had been flat since about update 250, and new subfamilies had slowed to a few per hundred updates.

A.3 The subfamilies

Subfamilies are the coarse contact types of Section 6; they are coarse descriptions, not proved components. Components: the path groups of Section 14. Distinct: static scenes further apart than 5 mm or 3° from each other. A disturbance test of the subfamilies is not included: it has not been run yet.

A.4 The same solver without births and deaths, and without the type term

Two runs from the same start isolate the two mechanisms, the type term of Section 7 and the births and deaths of Section 8: one with the type term in the consensus score but without births and deaths, and one with neither. Their spread over contact types is shown in A.2. A ten-second comparison of their consensus points at a common update is not included: it has not been run yet.

A.5 Measurements behind the formulation

The gap between the bodies. The first version of the contact term used a general-purpose distance between the convex pieces of the two bodies. Moving the spoon by \(10^{-7}\) m changed that distance by up to 73 mm, and on seven scenes it reported contact although the bodies were 1.2 to 39 mm apart. The gap of Section 5, from exact signed distances of the primitives on the other body's samples, changes by less than a micrometre under the same moves and agrees with the dense samples where both are defined.

The contact term. Without it, the spoon lying apart from the mug on the table was the largest resting family: about two particles in five ended there in the runs before it. With it, the share of particles not in contact at the end of the release fell to 3 to 4 %, and every consensus point that passes the ten-second check here is in contact.

Births and deaths. On a saved population, the calibrated rate gave 96 deaths against 100 expected; deaths occurred only in over-represented types and parents only in under-represented ones; no fine type was emptied; and the copied rows equal their parents'. With the step switched off, the same program reproduces the run without births and deaths bit for bit over its first updates. The step itself takes about 0.01 s per update.

Copies of falling particles do not help. In this run, six of the 24 touching types had particles only while those particles were still falling: no particle in them was ever at rest, their objective was 34 to 50 mm, and of the 15 copies the births made into them, 13 had left within one update. The births help a type only once a particle rests in it, so they keep families that the population has found rather than finding new ones.

The read-out at update 372. The run decodes its consensus points only at its last planned update, and it was stopped earlier. The consensus points were therefore read out by evaluating the saved state of update 372 once more, with the same program and without a further step. The particles' scenes, objectives, rest scores and gaps agree with the run's saved values bit for bit; the consensus weights agree to the tolerance of the effective-sample-size solve (median effective sample size 2.9994 against 3.0000), because the run's warm start of \(\alpha_i\) was not saved.

Samples of the wall correction. With 64 samples of the spoon the correction of Section 4 is 15 % too large at the median, against a reference of 4096 samples; with 256 to 2048 samples the error is 0.3 to 1.7 %. The run uses 2048.

A.6 Numerical realisation of the dynamics

The particle equations are stepped with Euler–Maruyama at \(\Delta t=0.1\), with all coefficients evaluated at the start of the step. The attitude moves along the great circle given by the tangent step, \(u\leftarrow\cos\|v\|\,u+\sin\|v\|\,v/\|v\|\). The offset is re-expressed in the plane of the new attitude by orthogonal projection, keeping its length, and reflected at the collar boundary: a length \(r\gt1\) becomes \(2-r\). The spoon's rotation is updated by the drift and then by the noise, \(R\leftarrow R\exp(\Delta t\,\widehat{\omega})\exp(\widehat{\eta})\); the two exponentials keep it on \(SO(3)\), and taking the drift first avoids mixing it with a large roll of the noise inside one exponential. The order coordinate is recorded by its sign when the scene is built. Every moved particle's scene then receives a release evaluation, ready to form the scores, the contact types, the births and deaths and the consensus of the next update.

The shaped noise needs the metric's Cholesky factor at each particle and the drift \(b\), which takes fourteen further evaluations of the closed-form metric per particle. The measured time per update at 10 000 particles was 12 s at the median: 8.1 s for the releases, 2.6 s for the scene map, and 0.6 s for the consensus, including the wall correction and the solve for \(\alpha_i\); the births and deaths take about 0.01 s.

A.7 The same solver with 50 000 particles

The same solver was run with 50 000 particles from the same seed for the same 372 updates, and its consensus points received the same ten-second check and the same path search. 33 365 of them pass the check, 33 363 of them in contact, in 18 subfamilies, against 17 here; the subfamily that appears only with more particles is tilted, against, which is reached at every update with 10 000 particles but never comes to rest. The path search over both runs together finds 779 groups: 64 are shared by both runs, 553 contain only scenes of the larger run, and 162 contain only scenes of this run; 4 groups of this run were merged by paths through scenes of the larger run. More particles therefore add many more tested components, while each run alone still leaves some of the other's unreached. The effective number of subfamilies over the static points is 13.7 against 13.3. These are finite path searches on one seed.
